subject: Answers to: songbird data with questions on adjustment selection

messages.subject: Answers to: songbird data with questions on adjustment selection
parts:
Thank you for your responses to my plea for help. Listed below are the =
answers I received on my adjustment selection and variance question ("I am =
using distance to analyze transects to determine avian abundance (analyzed =
in clusters) in agricultural fields. I have tried multiple truncations, =
groupings, and models and have come up with 'best' models for each =
treatment/time period. I originally used the default 'sequential' for =
adjustment terms and 'estimate variance empirically' for variance. Should =
I go back and try the 'forward' adjustment selection and bootstrap for =
variance? I know Distance Sampling (pg120) recommends evaluating the =
bootstrap on the final model, but is this always a superior method of =
estimating variance? I have noticed, for the few that I have already =
tried, that the CV for bootstrap is higher than the CV for the analytical. =
Is this normal?")

1. I would not bother with forward selection. It was originally put in =
the code for research sake. Also, you didn't say what you did regarding =
truncation but don't use AIC to select between different truncation points =
because as the data differs so does the likelihood and it has nothing to =
do with the model. What happens with the variance on a bootstrap depends =
on your data and sampling. The traditional variance using the squared =
cv's of each component assumes independence between the various components =
(detection, encounter rate, and group size). If these are not independent =
then the bootstrap variance can either go up or down but typically down =
because the covariance between n and f(0) is negative. If f(0) goes up it =
is because animals are less
detectable and therefore n goes down. This can happen when your are =
sampling different habitats but have not stratified. Imagine what would =
happen if some lines were in grassland and others in forested areas. =
Likewise, you can get a covariance between group size and the number of =
groups. If you get some areas in which there are few larger groups and =
other areas in which there are more smaller groups then there is a =
negative covariance between n and E(S). The other difference bt the =
bootstrap and the std variance is the latter is conditioned on the model =
which includes both the choice of key and adjustment functions and the =
number of adjustments. If you bootstrapped and included multiple =
estimators then the bootstrap variance will incorporate model
selection uncertainty which will inflate the variance. The bootstrap =
variance will be more relaible as long as you are not getting a lot of =
fitting errors during the bootstrapping. This can occur occasionally if =
you include the hazard rate model.

Hope this helps

Jeff Laake
2.
> >I am using distance to analyze transects to determine avian abundance=20
> >(analyzed in clusters) in agricultural fields. I have tried multiple
> >truncations, groupings, and models and have come up with 'best' models =
for=20
> >each treatment/time period. I originally used the default 'sequential' =
for=20
> >adjustment terms and 'estimate variance empirically' for variance. =
Should=20
> >I go back and try the 'forward' adjustment selection

If you have "good" distance data (ie wide shoulder, smooth decline in=20
detection function) then it is unlikely to make much, if any difference. =
In=20
theory 'forward' adjustment selection is more flexible than sequential=20
selection of adjustment terms, as it tests all potential adjustment terms =
to=20
see which is "best" to add next. In fact, I'm not sure why this isn't =
the=20
default in Distance! -- I guess because (a) it is computationally more=20
intensive and (b) generally, for "good" data, you won't want/need to =
fit=20
high-order adjustment terms. Maybe one of the other distance sampling =
gurus=20
can shed some light on this? Anyway, as I said, it shouldn't make much=20
difference.

> > and bootstrap for variance? I know Distance Sampling (pg120) recommends=
=20
> >valuating the bootstrap on the final model, but is this always a =
superior=20
> >method of estimating variance? I have noticed, for the few that I =
have=20
> >already tried, that the CV for bootstrap is higher than the CV for the=20
> >analytical. Is this normal? Thanks for the help.

It is superior in that it makes fewer assumptions, and admits more real=20
sources of uncertainty. =20

For fewer assumptions: you don't use the analytic variance estimate of =
f(0),=20
so you are not relying on the assumption that observations are independant=
=20
(although this assumptions still plays a role in selection of adjustment=20=

terms). If you use the percentile-based confidence limits you are also =
not=20
making any assumption about the distribution of the density estimate =
(the=20
parametric confidence limits assume it is log-normally distributed). =20

For more uncertainty, you are including the uncertainty due to selecting=20=

adjustment terms. You can also put in more than one key function =
(Model=20
Definition | Detection Function | Models, + button) to include uncertainty=
=20
due to selecting which key function to use. You will end up with wider=20
confidence limits, but they will more accurately reflect your true=20
uncertainty. For more on model selection uncertainty, see:

Buckland, Burnham and Augustin. 1997. Model Selection: An Integral Part =
of=20
Inference. Biometrics 53: 603-618.

and part of

Burnham and Anderson. 1998. Model Selection and Inference. Springer =
Verlag.

One time that bootstrapping is a bad idea is when you only have a small=20
number of points or lines to bootstrap. Ideally you want at least =
15-20=20
points or lines before you consider using bootstrapping -- otherwise =
your=20
results will likely be quite unreliable. This also applies to using =
points=20
or lines to give an empirical estimate of encounter rate variance.

Hope this helps,

- Len Thomas
